newsitem.title: UK: IRA van contained explosives, bomb equipment.
newsitem.headline: IRA van contained explosives, bomb equipment.

text.p: A van abandoned by the Irish Republican Army near a Belfast hotel earlier this week contained 1,000 lbs (450 kg) of explosives, police said on Thursday.

Late on Tuesday British security forces sealed off parkland around Belfast Castle, a 19th century former private mansion packed with revellers, as bomb disposal officers tried to establish if the vehicle contained explosives.
Police said they had also found other bomb-making equipment in the vehicle apart from the home-made explosives.
"It contained about 1,000 lbs of explosives in two bins, also detonating cord and other bomb-making equipment," a police spokesman said.
Security forces are cautious when directed towards targets by the IRA, as they have been caught out by booby traps and secondary bombs in the past.

Police said a man using an IRA identity codeword had telephoned the media late on Tuesday saying there was a landmine in the vehicle. He said the group had dumped the vehicle after encountering high-level British counter-guerrilla activity.
A senior police officer said the incident was not unexpected in the current security climate.

"We have been warning for some time of the likelihood of terrorist attacks and have taken steps to counter the efforts of paramilitary groups to inflict death and destruction," said Chief Superintendent William Davidson of the Royal Ulster Constabulary.

Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew on Wednesaday described the IRA's action as "a New Year message" from what he called criminal gangsters who had not turned away from a strategy of violence to achieve their political objectives.
Police said officers on high alert during renewed tension had already become suspicious of a van parked in the hotel grounds and called in the bomb squad.
A bride and groom, their guests and others attending New Year's Eve receptions were among those led out of the building.
Security has been stepped up across Northern Ireland and in mainland Britain since the IRA abandoned a ceasefire last February in a 27-year campaign to end British rule.
The IRA set off a wave of bombs in British cities and killed a soldier at British army headquarters south of Belfast last October, dashing hopes of an early end to violence.

Tension increased recently with signs that pro-British Loyalist guerrillas might end a two-year truce. Booby trap bombs were placed under cars belonging to senior republicans, injuring one of them. Loyalist hardliners were blamed.
